concept.name: FX swap
concept.definition: A contract combining a spot purchase (sale) of one currency against another with a simultaneous offsetting forward sale (purchase) of the same amounts. In the spot leg one party lends one currency and borrows the other at the spot rate; in the forward leg the exchange is reversed at a pre-agreed forward rate, making the instrument economically similar to collateralized borrowing and lending. FX swaps were the most traded FX instrument, at $3.8 trillion per day (51% of global turnover) in April 2022.
concept.intuition: An FX swap is like a repo with a currency instead of a security: you swap currencies today and swap them back later at a pre-set rate.
concept.mechanics: Because the two legs offset, an FX swap creates no net open currency position; its price is the difference between the forward and spot legs, quoted in forward (swap) points that reflect the interest rate differential plus any cross-currency basis. Typical maturities are very short — instruments maturing within a week accounted for about 70% of FX swap turnover in April 2022 — and the instrument is used for funding liquidity management, hedging and rolling forward positions.
concept.formula: Swap cost is quoted as forward points = F - S, with F = S x (1 + r_q x T) / (1 + r_b x T) under covered interest parity; S = spot, F = forward rate, r_q and r_b = quote- and base-currency interest rates, T = tenor.
concept.failure_modes: FX swap markets are vulnerable to funding squeezes — during the 2008 crisis and March 2020 dollar borrowers faced sharply higher rates when lenders stepped back. Persistent deviations from covered interest parity (the cross-currency basis) mean swap-implied funding costs can differ materially from cash-market rates.
concept.misconceptions: An FX swap is not a bet on the exchange rate (the legs offset, so there is no open FX position), and it differs from a cross-currency swap, a longer-term instrument that also exchanges periodic interest payments.
concept.example: A Dutch pension fund borrows dollars and lends euros in the spot leg of a 3-month FX swap, then repays the dollars and receives back euros in the forward leg at the pre-agreed rate, hedging its dollar assets without an open currency position.
